transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-02-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 mins
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Kenji (Redwood SE), Lena (BrightLayer Product), Arjun (BrightLayer Eng), Priya (BrightLayer Security), Tom (BrightLayer ops)

Summary:
Quick hosted API orientation focusing on streamed chat generation basics, recommended parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), streaming behavior, and retry/fallback strategies for a health-care customer with sensitive data constraints. Covered hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs and what to expect in Console for observability.

Topics:
- Getting started with hosted chat generation (API call shape and streaming)
- Typical parameter choices and cost/latency tradeoffs
- Retry/backoff patterns and idempotency considerations
- Data residency, encryption, and SOC2 notes for Private/Dedicated options
- Console tour (latency charts, token cost breakdown, traces)

Action items (also in metadata): referenced above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um quick intro, i'm maya from redwood inference, and with me is kenji our se who will do the console demo and a quick bench. 
[00:06] Lena: hi thanks, excited — we've been evaluating a few options for in-app triage chat, want low latency and good accuracy, obviously PHI concerns for us.
[00:12] Kenji: great. i'll try to show the hosted api flow first then talk about fallbacks. apologies if the screen share is a bit laggy.
[00:20] Arjun: quick meta question — are we talking streaming end-to-end or batch generation?
[00:24] Maya: streaming primarily, yes. we find customers want partial tokens asap for UI snappyness; we'll cover tradeoffs.
[00:30] Kenji: ok starting with the basic request shape — you hit POST /v1/chat with model, messages, streaming=true, and you subscribe to delta tokens. sometimes auto-transcript will write model as "redwood-chat" or similar — ignore that, it's a generic label.
[00:45] Kenji: for params, temperature 0.0-0.3 for deterministic triage, max_tokens depending on prompt, and top_p usually left at 1.0. for cost concerns you can cap max_tokens and use stop sequences.
[01:05] Lena: when you say deterministic, do you mean we should force temp=0? we've seen hallucinations with lower temps sometimes.
[01:11] Maya: yeah that's common — lower temp reduces randomness but doesn't fix hallucination; you still need instruction engineering and few-shot context. also quality monitoring (console/evals) helps catch regressions.
[01:20] Arjun: what about latency and batching — if we set streaming true does that reduce throughput?
[01:26] Kenji: streaming is orthogonal to batching; server side batches may still aggregate token work, but streaming gets partials earlier. for high throughput we recommend response-level batching on our Dedicated pool or using our Optimize suggestions for batching window.
[01:40] Priya: security note — how is the data retained? we need clarity on retention for PHI.
[01:45] Maya: good callout — hosted retains request/response for 30 days by default for debugging, but we have options: opt-out retention, or go Dedicated/Private where logs are customer-managed. we'll share SOC2 docs and the retention settings.
[01:58] Priya: ok please send details and the network diagram.
[02:02] Kenji: jumping into a quick Console view — (screen: Console -> Model routes). here you can see per-route latency p50/p95, token cost heatmap, and tracing hooks where you can correlate tokens to requests. sometimes the auto-capture names show up wrong — like the route may be called "chat-gen-1" in the console clip.
[02:20] Kenji: here's a live request stream, watch the deltas come in. note the SSE connection — if a connection drops, client should fall back to non-streaming or re-try with the message idempotency token.
[02:33] Arjun: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern? exponential? jitter?
[02:37] Kenji: yes — exponential backoff with capped max attempts. best practice: 1) try a fast reconnect for transient TCP resets, 2) if you get a 429 or 503, backoff with jitter and attempt to call a fallback model (cheaper / smaller) for degraded mode. also use idempotency tokens for any calls that change state.
[02:55] Maya: important: streaming doesn't guarantee every token will arrive if the connection dies; we recommend the client keep a sequence of partials and resume logic. customers sometimes send a short summary of the partial to a persistent store and then continue.
[03:10] Lena: hm for our UX we need to show partial suggestions and allow user to accept mid-stream. any concerns about cost if partials are long?
[03:16] Kenji: cost is per token produced; partials don't change that. but you can set max_tokens to limit worst case lengths. also prefix caching and KV cache helps for repeated context — but quick note: transcriptions sometimes say KV cash which is a common mis-typing in notes.
[03:30] Priya: can we mask PHI before sending? we'd prefer pre-filtering in the client.
[03:35] Maya: absolutely, client-side redaction is recommended; if you need server-side PII scrubbing we have partners for that. we'll include guidance in the quickstart.
[03:42] Kenji: switching to params — temperature, top_p, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty. for deterministic triage we usually recommend temp 0.0-0.2 and presence_penalty 0.0, but for creative rewrites increase temp and maybe top_p lower to shift mass.
[03:58] Arjun: does streaming interact with decoding strategies like sampling vs beam search?
[04:02] Kenji: streaming typically uses token-sampling decoding; beam search is less common for autoregressive streaming APIs. if you need beams, you often run a non-streaming pass.
[04:12] Maya: ok quick demo of a retry scenario — i'm going to trigger a 503 by throttling the client. (pause) you'll see the client back off and then attempt fallback to a smaller model "redwood-lite" which returns a shorter summary.
[04:32] (audio: keyboard, slight crosstalk)
[04:35] Tom: question — fallback to smaller model, does that change signature/formatting? we want consistent JSON output for downstream services.
[04:41] Kenji: good question. best practise is to use a normalizer layer — keep the same system prompt and a small post-process step. also Redwood supports structured output / function calling to enforce JSON shapes which helps across fallbacks. note: sometimes function calling metadata shows up as "func-calling" in transcripts.
[04:58] Lena: can you show how to set streaming timeouts and client-side reconnection?
[05:02] Kenji: yes, timeout on the socket ~ 30s of inactivity, then reconnect with exponential jitter. if you reconnect you can optionally send the last message id and model position to resume — we provide a resume token in some SDKs. 
[05:20] Arjun: re: rate limits — if we have bursts from many users, what's the best way to preserve user experience?
[05:25] Maya: route-level rate limits in the Console help, plus client-side local queuing and token-bucket smoothing. if you expect high QPS, Dedicated capacity or reserved pools can guarantee throughput.
[05:36] Priya: customers often ask for VPC/private deployment — what's the gap between Hosted and Private?
[05:40] Maya: Hosted: fastest to start, usage billing, limited retention controls; Dedicated: reserved GPU pools, data isolation and SLA; Private: VPC or on-prem with customer-managed control plane and stricter KMS/HSM integration. for PHI, Private or Dedicated with strict retention is common.
[05:58] Lena: what are common latency numbers? we need p95 < 700ms for short prompts.
[06:03] Kenji: depends on model and sequence length. smaller models on Dedicated can reach p95 ~200-400ms for short prompts; hosted p95 for base models often 400-900ms. we'll run a sample bench with your prompts and share the p50/p95.
[06:17] Arjun: that'd be great — can you include GPU type or region in the bench?
[06:21] Kenji: yes i'll include region and instance type. also note quantized variants exist so you can trade a little quality for big cost wins.
[06:30] Priya: security again — SSO/SAML and audit logs?
[06:33] Maya: we support SAML SSO for Console, RBAC, API keys, and audit logs. Dedicated/Private include more granular audit retention and KMS. we'll attach SOC2 and our security whitepaper.
[06:45] Mike (customer audio slight): sorry i'm late, any notes on idempotency tokens?
[06:48] Kenji: idempotency token is recommended for any stateful action — not all generation calls need it, but if you persist outputs or charge a user, include one. it helps dedupe retries.
[06:57] Lena: do you have examples of error handling code?
[07:00] Kenji: yes — our SDKs include retry helpers for common patterns; i'll paste node/python snippets in the follow-up repo. typical pattern: if connection reset -> quick reconnect; 429/503 -> exponential backoff + fallback to cheaper model; others -> surfacing to the UI.
[07:14] Maya: ok let's do a short live run — arjun shared a triage prompt. we'll stream it and force a reconnect to show behavior.
[07:20] (demo running, some delay)
[07:40] Kenji: see partials arriving. at 07:55 i'll kill the socket.
[07:55] (sound) 
[08:00] Kenji: socket closed; client retried per policy and resumed with resume token, resulting in short gap but the UI can fill from cached partials.
[08:10] Arjun: looks good. 
[08:12] Priya: one more security thing — key rotation and HSM integration for private keys?
[08:16] Maya: yes support for KMS and HSM, and we can show recommended rotation cadence. for Dedicated/Private you can bring your own KMS.
[08:26] Lena: timeline question — we want to go to pilot in 6 weeks, is that realistic?
[08:31] Maya: yes pilot is realistic — steps: quickstart + sample bench this week, security review next week, pilot contract for Dedicated or hosted pilot in 4-6 weeks.
[08:40] Kenji: we'll also add an Optimize run to recommend batching and quantization levels for your workload. that usually yields 20-40% unit cost reduction.
[08:50] Tom: what's typical pilot success criteria?
[08:53] Maya: p95 latency, cost per session, accuracy on your evaluation prompt set, and security signoff. we'll work with you to define pass/fail thresholds.
[09:02] Lena: ok last question — can Console alert when token costs spike?
[09:05] Kenji: yes alerting by route and model; we can set thresholds on tokens per minute and anomalies based on baseline.
[09:12] Maya: all right sounds like a plan. recap: we'll send quickstart repo + console recording + security docs; kenji will run bench with your prompts and return p50/p95 and cost estimates; priya will send requirements and we'll slot a security review next week.
[09:29] Priya: thanks. also please include an architecture diagram for private deployment options.
[09:35] Maya: we'll do that — i'll include the diagram and SOC2 artifacts.
[09:38] Lena: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[09:40] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in thread with the artifacts and schedule.

End of transcript.

References shared in chat: quickstart repo link (link posted), Console recording (link), Security whitepaper (link). Some auto-generated notes mis-typed product names (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" vs Dedicated).

Caveats on transcription: occasional mis-recognition of acronyms (KMS sometimes shown as "kms" or "k m s"), and proper nouns like BrightLayer appear as "Bright Layer" in a few segments.
